title: Home — Jon D. Elton
text: Jon D. Elton — Thoughts & Muses of the Man. A singer, poet, and family man. Here you will find various aspects of my life I wish to make public. The Lake House at Sudden Valley on Lake Whatcom, a favourite gathering place for all of us. D.H. Elton Poems — popular poems written by my father's father, a prolific poet who wrote hundreds of them. My Desiderata — the affirmation I recite to myself every day, things worth desiring in this life. Thoughts & Poems — a compilation of thoughts and poems I have collected during my life. Music — songs and performances in one place, a lifelong singer's collection. Family — Jon & Mary's family, six grown children, their spouses, and fifteen grandchildren. Gems from Jon — a monthly letter of poems, reflections, and musings, straight from my heart to yours. Feed & Teach a Child — part of every gift goes toward helping underprivileged children in Africa.

title: The Elton Lake House
text: The Elton Lake House at Sudden Valley, Lake Whatcom, Bellingham, Washington. Enjoy the waterfront of beautiful Lake Whatcom — waterski, swim, kayak, canoe, or just read a book. Located at #6 Inlet Circle, Bellingham, in Sudden Valley on Lake Whatcom. A 4,200 square foot home with 5 bedrooms and 4½ bathrooms, including a self-contained suite on the lowest level. It has been a great family reunion location for our family of 6 grown children, their spouses, and 15 grandchildren. Pretty tight when we are all there at the same time — but it's great having everyone under one roof. Kind words from our friends: the Walker Family, Cordell & Marilyn Rolfson, and Merlin & Maureen Smith.

title: D.H. Elton Poems — Collection
text: Poems written by my father's father, David Horton Elton. Grandpa wrote a lot of great poems — literally hundreds of them. He wrote poems for important events in the lives of his wife and children, for his Kiwanis Club, his Liberal Party, his Church, his City. He would write a poem for a friend or neighbour in need, or an event he was asked to speak at. He was very prolific and could write a poem at least every week. Many of his poems became classics that have been memorized and passed on. The popular poems include Guy in the Glass, Life the True Poem, My Sweetheart, Teach Me to Love, My Mother, God's Choicest Gift, Three Things, and Mother Bobbed Her Hair Today. More poems are being transcribed from Grandpa's journals. Check back soon.

title: My Desiderata
text: My Desiderata — Desiderata, Latin for Desired Things. It came out of a business trip to Calgary many years ago, when I stayed with my cousin Pamela Lehto in her lovely town house. On the wall of her guest bathroom was a plaque with Desiderata by Max Ehrmann. I remembered it from back in 1971, when a spoken word version by Les Crane was played on the radio and made it to #8 on the Billboard chart of the day, #4 in Canada. I committed it to memory, and over the years found a few bits I didn't like so much that I left out, and added a number of my own thoughts — making it Our Desiderata. I recite it to myself pretty much every day, most often during my morning shower. Go calmly amid the noise and haste and remember what peace may be found in silence. As far as possible, without surrender, be on good terms with all persons. Speak your truth quietly and clearly, and listen to others, even those who can do nothing to you, or for you, for they too have their story, and you just never know. If you compare yourself to others, you may become vain or bitter, for always there will be those greater and lesser than yourself. Enjoy your achievements as well as your plans. Keep interested in your own career, however humble, it's a real possession in the changing fortunes of time. Exercise caution in your business affairs, for the world is full of trickery, but let that not blind you to the virtue there is, for many seek after high ideals and everywhere, life is full of heroism. Be yourself, especially do not feign affection or be cynical about love, for in the face of all aridity and disenchantment it is as perennial as the grass. Take kindly the counsel of the years, gracefully surrendering the things of youth. Nurture strength of spirit that it may shield you from sudden misfortune, but do not distress yourself with dark imaginings. Many fears are born from fatigue, misunderstanding and loneliness. And when facing hardships move through them quickly, for the longer we dwell on our misfortunes, the greater is their power to do us damage. Beyond a wholesome discipline, be gentle with yourself, for you are a child of the universe, no less than the trees and the stars, you have a right to be here. And whether or not it is clear to you, no doubt the universe is unfolding as it should. Therefore be at peace with God, whatever you conceive Him to be. And whatever your fears or aspirations in this busy confused world, keep peace in your soul, for all its shame, drudgery and broken dreams, it is still a beautiful world. Be cheerful, be a good friend, be forgiving, for we all need forgiveness and remember it is usually more important to the giver than to the receiver. Be grateful and show it. Be generous to a fault. Have faith, it's what gives us hope! Don't take yourself too seriously, and strive to be happy, it is a choice.

title: Thoughts & Poems
text: Thoughts & Poems is a compilation of thoughts and poems I have collected during my life. Lots of great thoughts there, and it is searchable. From favorite verses to quiet reflections, this is a growing archive of what has moved me along the way — shared here in the hope that something might move you too. title: Pottery
text: Pottery — Hands in the clay, poems in three dimensions. Why a poet makes pots: pottery found me later in life, and there is something honest about a lump of mud. It asks you to be patient, to listen, to give — and then to let go, and let the fire have the last word. Words about the wheel: clay is the most patient listener I know; a pot is a poem you can hold; centering the clay is centering yourself; if the middle holds, the rest will follow; every piece comes out of the kiln either a little more or a little less than you hoped, and both are gifts. How a piece comes to life: centering, throwing, glazing, firing. From the studio: ancient pots, neolithic pottery, a Maya polychrome vase, the everyday bowl, and the wheel that started it all.

title: Guy in the Glass
text: Guy in the Glass. We always thought grandpa had written this poem but maybe he didn't. Great poem either way. When you've got all you want in your struggle for pelf, and the world crowns you king for a day, then go to the mirror and look at yourself, and see what that guy has to say. For it isn't your father, or mother, or wife, who judgment upon you must pass. But the fellow whose verdict counts most in your life, is that guy staring back from the glass. He's the fellow to please, never mind all the rest, for he'll be with you clear to the end. And you've passed your most difficult dangerous test, when the man in the glass is your friend. You may be like Jack Horner and chisel a plum, and think you're a wonderful guy, but the man in the glass says, you're only a bum, if you can't look him straight in the eye. You may fool all the world down the pathway of years, and get pats on your back as you pass. But your final reward will be heartache and tears, if you have cheated the Guy in the Glass.

title: Life, the True Poem
text: Life, the True Poem. Let my life be the poem I'd write, let it plead for me day after day. Never mind what my pen may indite, never mind what my feeble lips say. What I do is a heart-felt refrain. What I am is the standard and test. The rhythm of action is plain, the poem I live is the best. Let me BE let me DO let me LIVE, the poem my LIFE may inspire. Let me Strive, let me Serve, let me GIVE, the Highest my Soul can Desire. By David H. Elton.

title: My Sweetheart
text: My Sweetheart. I see you, as in former years, 'mid laughter, sadness, joys and tears, through shade and sunshine, faith and fears, the star of hope — time but endears — MY SWEETHEART. And babies, as the years roll on, with merry chatter, cheery song, have helped us on the way along, recalling days when we were young — MY SWEETHEART. I sometimes wonder how we'd fare, if we were just a childless pair, no boys or girls our lives to share, no children, dear, to love and care — MY SWEETHEART. It seems to me we'd miss a heap of real joy, and gladness sweet, which only boys and girls entreat, to help o'ercome the cares we meet — MY SWEETHEART. You're still as sweet, so runs my plea, as that blest day in Tennessee, when just Seventeen you did agree, to have this photo made for me — MY SWEETHEART. I've cherished it through all the years, faith's precious gift, dispelling fears, symbol of love — life's glad arrears, hope's blessed rainbow through the tears — MY SWEETHEART.

title: Teach Me to Love
text: Teach Me to Love. Four little words, a simple phrase, that falls like dew on sleeping flower, or like the sun's effulgent rays, bestowing service every hour. For in these simple words, I find the light and wisdom from above — the essence of all good, combined in these four words: Teach me to love. Teach me to love with heart sincere, devoid of all dissimulation. A love that gladly volunteers to serve, without remuneration. For in such love, as I conclude, we lift our thoughts to heaven above in gentle, joyful rectitude expressed in faith: Teach me to love. Teach me to love, both here and now, humanity as one great whole. Who waits upon the when and how will lose the race and miss the goal. Loving and serving, day by day, with humble grace, in semblance of our hope — the light, the truth, the way, still guided by: Teach me to love.

title: My Mother
text: My Mother. Guardian of Baby-hood, Boy-hood, and Youth. Champion of Virtue, and Honour and Truth. Friend of my Manhood — eternal friend, aye, her spirit and influence bless me, each day — MY MOTHER. In the Mansions of Glory, a friend is she. With the Sanctified Hosts she is pleading for me. She links me with Heaven, with God, and His will, she was always my friend and my friend she is still — MY MOTHER. Death does not finish her mission of Love, she zealously labours in regions above — there through all time and eternity, her love shall endure, and forever she'll be — MY MOTHER. By D.H. Elton, 1935. This is a photo of Isabella Amelia Elton with her son Hyrum, Grandpa's brother, and his two daughters.

title: God's Choicest Gift
text: God's Choicest Gift. God gave us the Sunshine, the Rain, and the Showers, He gave us the Springtime, the Fields, and the Flowers. He gave us the Summer, the birds on the wing. He gave them their Music, He taught them to Sing. He gave us the Seasons, in order they roll — the Autumn, the Winter, perfecting the whole. All Nature declaring His Glory and Power, with the sweet singing bird, and the blossoming flower. But the Choicest of Gifts, by His bounteous hand given, the finest bestowed in Earth or in Heaven, is the great Mother-love, I'm sure there's no other, as needful, and helpful, and faithful, as MOTHER. 1930.

title: Three Things
text: Three Things. Written for my youngest son, John Dalton Elton, on the occasion of his 14th Birthday, February 27th, 1934, at home. Born February 27th, 1920. Three things, my son, to help you on. They all come from within. The first I'll state, a virtue great, is called SELF-DISCIPLINE. For number two, I transmit you, a grace none should neglect — just like its mate, a grand estate, we'll call it SELF-RESPECT. And number three, you'll plainly see, cast in the self same mold — a moral will to conquer ill, is rightly SELF-CONTROL. Keep these in mind, and you will find true happiness and joy. They'll premiums pay in every way, big dividends, my boy.

title: Mother Bobbed Her Hair Today
text: Mother Bobbed Her Hair Today. These verses were written to my daughter, Viva, then in Bangor, Maine, U.S.A., February 12th, 1925 — the day of the decapitation. Mother bobbed her hair today, yes, she did, and daughter, say don't let on, but really she doesn't look too bad to me. Sort of curious like, by heck, where the clippers trimmed her neck, don't know yet just what to say: mother bobbed her hair today. She came in the parlour, stood beside my easy chair, sort o' stroked me on the chin, then she gently started in: Dearie, do you like my hair? I looked 'round with solemn stare; couldn't tell if I'd been shot, whether it was bobbed or not. Then she laughed, I looked again; sure enough, it was quite plain. Tresses gone, I changed my mind — dinky, kinky curls behind. Made out I was sore and vexed, angry, hurt, and much perplexed. But 'twas done, what could I say: mother bobbed her hair today. Why do women bob their hair? Don't ask me, for I declare I don't know, but here's some guesses why they bob their pretty tresses; maybe it's because they're fearful they'll be called old Rip Van Winkle, covered wagon, horse and mane, or some prehistoric Jane. Then they come to you, confessing that it saves a lot of dressing; night and morning, so 'tis said, all they do is shake their head.
